Price volatility is a measure of how difficult it is at any given moment to suppress the knowledge that no one knows anything. Here's this week’s view. Our perspectives on where crude demand meets supply are always by degrees of separation. This relationship between physical and paper oil is the subject of a newsletter by University of Lausanne professor Gianluca Benigno<https://substack.com/redirect/6a166454-7449-4b41-a61b-be5088eefaa8?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Prompted by reports that the US Treasury wants to combat price spikes by shorting oil futures<https://substack.com/redirect/43478fcd-0011-475a-8e7a-f59986ac99cd?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, Benigno explains that contract pricing hangs on confidence about delivery. Dependable supply is the only way to underpin that confidence. And while suppressing front-end futures prices could reduce the incentive to hoard, the only hoarding that happens during an oil shock is for need, not greed; each useful barrel “begins to trade less like a commodity and more like insurance”, he says. Meanwhile, over at Reuters, columnist Clyde Russell highlights that cash-settled Dubai cargoes are trading at a wide premium to the equivalent swaps<https://substack.com/redirect/eceaa806-df80-4ac0-bcca-aab425fd8563?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Paper traders are more confident than oil consumers about a quick ceasefire and manageable supply disruptions, which “seems untethered from the reality on the ground”, Russell says. To argue that a market is clearing at the wrong price is never not brave, but that’s particularly true when prices are moving like angry wasps in a Sodastream. In more predictable times, owning an oil future can be a hedge or a guarantee, whereas owning a barrel of crude before it’s needed is always a huge pain in the ass<https://substack.com/redirect/a61f9d02-7bd8-48db-8b2b-4372cf37ca19?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Premiums now being paid at the dock might be no more than a consequence of unpredictable times. There’s lots more to read on the theme but, honestly, unless you’re a Vitol trader or own a Lego factory, it’s OK not to bother. Commodity products are valued by what the buyer wants them for today, on known knowns. Those trying to guess what buyers will want tomorrow, on unknown unknowns, are asking for trouble. Of the two-dozen or so 2026 investment bank and fund manager outlooks<https://substack.com/redirect/182cf00b-6149-4053-b4f0-bea2aa9b8765?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> we collected in December, only a couple make passing reference to Iran, and none contain the word “Hormuz”. All of their forecasts are for crude to end the year gently up or range-bound. Don't get us wrong. Whether oil costs $60 or $120 a barrel is very important. But to the average person, whether first-month futures were $60 or $120 a barrel this morning is really only important for setting inflation expectations<https://substack.com/redirect/5c870f22-103b-43c4-82bd-d113ed31315f?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, which is what makes the Treasury plan to short them slightly less silly, though it’s still very very silly<https://substack.com/redirect/fe2376c1-7416-446e-9be1-a1f4505ace83?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Fuel price dependent, the money could be better spent on hiring skywriters to write “no one knows anything” in big letters each day over our major financial centres.
